Commentary.Commentary: Back for the chase. The Windies players are out in the middle. Paul Stirling and Andy Balbirnie to open for Ireland. Two slips in pace for Matthew Forde. Let's play...
...THE CHASE...

Some more good news! We have a RESTART TIME, and it is 3.30 pm GMT. Also, it will be a 46-over chase, and the revised target for Ireland will be 363 runs. Four bowlers are allowed to bowl a maximum of nine overs, and one can bowl their full quota of ten overs. The first Powerplay will be of nine overs, and the second one of 28 overs and the last one will be of nine overs again.

UPDATE - Positive news, folks! As they say, the weather is very unpredictable around here, and in a matter of minutes, the dark clouds have vanished and the sun is out now. The covers are going off and we could be getting back into action in a little while.

UPDATE - 3.08 pm GMT - The rain has ceased for now, but the covers remain on, and the Ireland chase has been officially delayed. There are a lot of dark clouds hovering above the ground, but we hope that we can get a result in this game. Stick with us for further news.

Uh..oh! Well, we might be in for a delayed restart, as it has started to pour in Dublin again. The covers have been brought on, but it is not a heavy shower as the ground staff are standing on the field near the covers. Stay tuned for further updates.

With this towering total on the board, and if the weather behaves and the rain stays away, West Indies bowlers will come out fired up, ready to close out the game and level up the series. They’ve got the cushion, the confidence, and the conditions on their side. Ireland, meanwhile, must now bring their A-game with the bat. They’ll need to forget the first innings and focus solely on the chase. The ask is enormous, but cricket has seen stranger things. Who will rise under pressure? Will Carty’s heroics be enough to seal it for the Windies, or can Ireland script a miraculous chase? Stay tuned, as the action for the second inning isn’t far away!

As for Ireland, they did have moments. Barry McCarthy struck early with two wickets in the Powerplay and ended with three overall, giving the West Indies a slight scare, but proved too expensive, as his spell was the most expensive one for an Irish bowler in ODIs ever. Andy Balbirnie removed Hope at the right time, and George Dockrell chipped in with a wicket too. But once the Carty-Hope partnership flourished, the pressure mounted, and the bowling looked flat. It wasn’t a terrible performance, but they didn’t maximise the early movement or maintain tight lines consistently. Captain Paul Stirling was forced to shuffle through seven bowling options, especially after debutant Jordan Neill left the field with a shoulder injury and couldn’t bowl a single delivery after that injury. Ireland also hurt themselves with sloppy fielding and extra deliveries; the No-Balls, Wides, and dropped chances added to the chaos and cost them heavily.

Carty reached his third ODI hundred, and second in the series, amidst rain delays, interruptions, and pressure. His focus didn’t waver for a moment. Even after two rain breaks, he came back with the same hunger and rhythm. He formed a 78-run partnership with Amir Jangoo, shouldering most of the scoring. After reaching his century, Carty exploded into beast mode, especially after being given a second life when Liam McCarthy bowled him off a No-Ball. That moment sparked an all-out assault. He went on to hit eight sixes in his innings, combining brute power with sublime timing. His 97-run stand with Justin Greaves came in just 40 balls, lifting West Indies past the 350 mark in no time. Carty finally fell for a sensational 170 off 142 balls, a knock that will be remembered for a long time. At the back end, Greaves also reached his maiden ODI fifty, playing a crucial cameo to power the Windies to a staggering total.

After being asked to bat first, West Indies had a shaky start, losing Brandon King on just the fourth ball of the match. Evin Lewis tried to counterattack with a few flashy shots, but his attempted slash on a wide delivery saw him walking back early, too. At 31/2, things were looking grim. But then came the familiar pairing, Keacy Carty and skipper Shai Hope, who once again steadied the ship. They built a solid platform with a 137-run stand, combining composure with calculated strokeplay. Hope played a fluent knock, scoring 75 off 75, while Carty settled in and took charge as the innings progressed. Carty’s innings was a masterclass in pacing. He began cautiously, respecting the conditions, but once he got in, he shifted gears beautifully, unleashing strokes all around the park.

West Indies have lit up the scoreboard with a colossal total of 385/7 runs in this must-win clash, trying to level the three-match ODI series at 1-1. With Ireland having won the first game and the second being washed out, this third match has become the decider, and the West Indies have come out with full authority. Their batting was sheer domination, and at the heart of it once again was the man in red-hot form, Keacy Carty, who has now scored back-to-back centuries in this series. He’s been nothing short of a rock, dependable, calm under pressure, and ruthlessly effective. While others batted around him, Carty was the anchor and the aggressor, both rolled into one. With such a commanding first-innings score, the Windies now have all the momentum.
